questions.statement: Complete the sentence: 'Please ___ until the meeting ends.'
questions.context: A classmate asks you to wait until an event finishes.

options.text: hold on
options.feedback: Correct. 'Hold on' means to wait briefly, which matches the request to wait until the meeting ends.

options.text: hold off
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Hold off' means to delay something or to keep away, which is a different meaning.

options.text: hold up
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Hold up' means to delay or to raise, which does not mean waiting.

options.text: hold out
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Hold out' means to resist or to extend something, neither of which fits waiting.

questions.explanation:
Basic phrasal verbs are memorised as units, so the correct preposition must be learned together with the verb.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: 'The launch will ___ until next month.'
questions.context: A manager explains that an action will be delayed.

options.text: be put on
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Put on' means to wear or to switch on, which has nothing to do with postponing.

options.text: be put off
options.feedback: Correct. 'Put off' means to postpone, and with a passive 'will be put off' the delay is described precisely.

options.text: be put in
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Put in' means to insert or to submit, which does not express postponement.

options.text: be put up
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Put up' means to erect or to display, which is unrelated to a delay.

questions.explanation:
Phrasal verbs change meaning entirely when the particle changes, so put off, put on and put up are unrelated in sense.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly means to stop doing something permanently.
questions.context: Two colleagues discuss giving up an activity.

options.text: She gave in her violin lessons last year.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Give in' means to surrender or to yield, which is not the same as stopping an activity by choice.

options.text: She gave off her violin lessons last year.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Give off' is not a standard phrasal verb in this meaning.

options.text: She gave up her violin lessons last year.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Give up' means to stop doing something, which matches stopping the lessons.

options.text: She gave out her violin lessons last year.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Give out' means to distribute or to emit, which does not fit.

questions.explanation:
Give up, give in and give out are distinct phrasal verbs whose particles each carry a different core meaning.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: 'Where has your brother ___ ? He was here an hour ago.'
questions.context: A friend arrives and asks about someone who is not present.

options.text: gone from
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Gone from' would work in some constructions but is incomplete without a stated reference point.

options.text: gone at
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Gone at' is not used to describe someone leaving.

options.text: gone in
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Gone in' is not a standard expression for leaving a place.

options.text: gone off
options.feedback: Correct. 'Gone off' means to have left the place, which fits a person who was present and is now absent.

questions.explanation:
The phrasal verb go off is used with people to describe departure, and its use with places differs.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly means the journey cost more than expected.
questions.context: A traveller describes an unexpected cost.

options.text: The trip cost me more than I had expected.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Cost me more' is the correct collocation, with the comparative 'more' rather than 'than' standing alone.

options.text: The trip cost more me than I had expected.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'More me' misplaces the indirect object, which must come directly after the verb.

options.text: The trip cost me more what I had expected.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'What' cannot replace the comparative 'more' in this structure.

options.text: The trip cost me than I had expected.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Than' cannot follow 'cost' without a comparative element before it.

questions.explanation:
A phrasal verb does not have to be separable, and some such as cost have a fixed structure that cannot be reorganised.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly says something is still waiting to be done.
questions.context: A report describes a task that has not been done yet.

options.text: I still have finish the report.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Have finish' omits the infinitive marker after the modal-like 'have to'.

options.text: I still have to finish the report.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Have to' plus the infinitive expresses an outstanding obligation, which is the intended meaning.

options.text: I still have the report to finish it.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'To finish it' adds a redundant object pronoun after an infinitive that already has its complement.

options.text: I still have to finishing the report.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Have to finishing' uses a gerund where the infinitive is required.

questions.explanation:
The structure have got to and have to both take the infinitive, so the verb after them is never inflected or made into a gerund.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly places the pronoun with a separable phrasal verb.
questions.context: A grammar task tests a separable phrasal verb with a pronoun object.

options.text: Please turn off them when you leave.
options.feedback: Wrong. A pronoun object must precede the particle, so 'off them' is incorrect.

options.text: Please turn the lights off when you leave.
options.feedback: Wrong. The particle form is possible with a noun object but is avoided when the object is a pronoun.

options.text: Please turn off the lights when you leave.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Please' selects the type form, in which the noun object comes before the particle, which is the standard and safer position.

options.text: Please turn the lights off it when you leave.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Off it' repeats the pronoun reference and does not fit the imperative request.

questions.explanation:
A separable phrasal verb allows either order with a noun object, but with a pronoun the pronoun must always come before the particle.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that uses the phrasal verb in its fixed position.
questions.context: A grammarian explains an inseparable phrasal verb.

options.text: I look my after younger brother every weekend.
options.feedback: Wrong. This scatters both the particle and the noun and produces no readable clause.

options.text: I look after my younger brother every weekend is true.
options.feedback: Wrong. The clause cannot be completed with 'is true' because it already contains its own structure.

options.text: I look my younger brother after every weekend.
options.feedback: Wrong. Separating the particle from the verb is not possible with an inseparable phrasal verb.

options.text: I look after my younger brother every weekend.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Look after' is inseparable, so the particle must stay directly after the verb and the object follows it.

questions.explanation:
Phrasal verbs fall into separable and inseparable types, and treating an inseparable one as separable is one of the commonest errors.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly means to change a date to a later one.
questions.context: A manager explains that a deadline has been rescheduled.

options.text: They put the deadline back by two weeks.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Put back' means to postpone, and with the noun object before the particle the sentence is standard.

options.text: They put back by the deadline two weeks.
options.feedback: Wrong. This version scatters the adverb and the noun and is not a well-formed sentence.

options.text: They put the deadline by back two weeks.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'By back' reverses the particle and the adverb that express the delay.

options.text: They put back the deadline by two weeks is fine.
options.feedback: Wrong. The clause cannot be extended with 'is fine' because 'they put back the deadline' has no direct object left.

questions.explanation:
'Put off' and 'put back' both express postponement, and with a noun object the particle may appear after it in standard English.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly means a plan did not happen.
questions.context: A traveller discovers that a plan has changed.

options.text: The trip fell over because of the strike.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Fell over' means to topple or to turn aside, which is a physical action.

options.text: The trip fell through because of the strike.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Fall through' means to fail to happen or be completed, which matches an abandoned plan.

options.text: The trip fell about because of the strike.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Fell about' means to laugh or struggle, which is unrelated to plans.

options.text: The trip fell in because of the strike.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Fell in' means to become enclosed or to arrive at a bad time, which does not mean a plan was cancelled.

questions.explanation:
Fall through, fall over and fall in are separate idioms whose particles cannot be swapped without changing the meaning entirely.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that means the student wants the explanation repeated.
questions.context: A student asks a teacher to explain something again.

options.text: Could you go off the explanation once more?
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Go off' means to leave or to explode, which is unrelated to reviewing material.

options.text: Could you go under the explanation once more?
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Go under' means to submerge or to examine in detail, which does not mean repeating something.

options.text: Could you go over the explanation once more?
options.feedback: Correct. 'Go over' means to review or repeat material, which is exactly what the student requests.

options.text: Could you go out the explanation once more?
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Go out' means to leave, and combining it with a noun in this way is not valid.

questions.explanation:
Go over, look over and read over all mean to review material, and the particle over carries that sense of a second reading.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly means to disagree verbally with a plan.
questions.context: A speaker reacts to a proposal by refusing to agree.

options.text: I can't go in with this plan.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Go in with' means to join in, which does not express disagreement.

options.text: I can't go for with this plan.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Go for' is not a phrasal verb in this meaning.

options.text: I can't go on with this plan.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Go on with' means to continue, so this would mean to continue the plan instead of opposing it.

options.text: I can't go along with this plan.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Go along with' means to agree or to cooperate, so 'can't go along with' means to disagree.

questions.explanation:
Negating a phrasal verb that expresses agreement is a standard way of expressing disagreement, so the particle must be exactly right.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly means something happened without warning.
questions.context: A report describes an event that happens unexpectedly.

options.text: The power cut out in the middle of the film.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Cut out' means to stop working or to be switched off, which describes a sudden loss of electricity.

options.text: The power cut over in the middle of the film.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Cut over' is not a standard expression for a power failure.

options.text: The power cut down in the middle of the film.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Cut down' means to reduce, which would suggest someone deliberately reduced the supply.

options.text: The power cut off in the middle of the film.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Cut off' can describe severing a connection but is not the usual verb for a power failure.

questions.explanation:
Cut out, cut off and cut down each describe a different kind of interruption, and the noun being interrupted narrows the correct choice.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly uses 'turn down'.
questions.context: An exam tests the difference between two phrasal verbs with the same verb.

options.text: Please turn down on the volume; it is too loud.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Turn down on' adds a preposition that is not part of the phrasal verb.

options.text: Please turn down the volume; it is too loud.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Turn down' means to reduce the intensity of something such as a sound or a flame, which fits the situation.

options.text: Please turn down the volume it is too loud.
options.feedback: Wrong. The two clauses run together without punctuation, so the sentence is malformed.

options.text: Please turn the down volume; it is too loud.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'The down volume' separates the adjective from the noun it modifies.

questions.explanation:
Turn down reduces intensity while turn off switches something off, and the object determines which sense applies.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly means to complete something before the required time.
questions.context: A student describes finishing a task early.

options.text: I finished the assignment ahead of the deadline it was.
options.feedback: Wrong. Adding a second clause after the phrase makes the sentence unbalanced and ungrammatical.

options.text: I finished the assignment off of time.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Off of' is not part of this phrase and changes the meaning to disconnection.

options.text: I finished the assignment ahead of time.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Ahead of time' is the fixed phrase for completing something earlier than expected.

options.text: I finished the assignment of ahead time.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Of ahead' reverses the two elements of the fixed expression.

questions.explanation:
Fixed phrases such as ahead of time, in advance and on time must be learnt as complete units and cannot be reorganised.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly means to get better after being ill.
questions.context: A report describes someone who has recovered from an illness.

options.text: He has got through at the flu at last.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Got through at' is not a valid combination and the preposition is misplaced.

options.text: He has got on the flu at last.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Get on' means to board or to manage, neither of which refers to illness.

options.text: He has got up the flu at last.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Get up' means to rise from bed, which describes an action rather than a recovery.

options.text: He has got over the flu at last.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Get over' means to recover from an illness or a difficulty, which matches the meaning of the sentence.

questions.explanation:
Get over and get through can both involve difficulty, but only get over means to recover from an illness.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the passive sentence with the correct phrasal verb.
questions.context: An exercise tests a phrasal verb in the passive.

options.text: The mistake was pointed out by the teacher.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Point out' means to draw attention to something, and 'was pointed out' correctly expresses that in the passive.

options.text: The mistake was pointed at by the teacher.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Pointed at' requires a target and is not used with a mistake as its object in this sense.

options.text: The mistake was pointed in by the teacher.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Pointed in' has no such meaning in English.

options.text: The mistake was pointed over by the teacher.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Pointed over' is not a valid form of this verb; over does not combine with point in this sense.

questions.explanation:
A phrasal verb in the passive keeps its particle immediately after the participle, so the whole unit is passivised together.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence preserves the idiomatic meaning of 'to put someone in their place'?
questions.context: A translator must choose between two renderings of an idiom.

options.text: She won the debate and outranked the room politely.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Outranked the room' is not English and attempts a literal rendering of the idiom.

options.text: She won the debate and reminded everyone of her seniority.
options.feedback: Correct. The idiom means to demonstrate that someone is less important than they believe, which the first sentence renders naturally.

options.text: She won the debate and raised her voice at the end.
options.feedback: Wrong. Raising the voice describes volume, not status, so it does not convey the idiom.

options.text: She won the debate and lowered the level of the discussion.
options.feedback: Wrong. Lowering the level of the discussion describes a different effect entirely.

questions.explanation:
A phrasal verb used as an idiom carries a figurative meaning that a literal rendering of its words almost always distorts.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly uses 'look into'.
questions.context: An exam tests a phrasal verb whose meaning depends on a final preposition.

options.text: The police are looking over the case into doubt.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Look over' means to review briefly and 'into doubt' is not a valid continuation.

options.text: The police are looking on the case.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Look on' means to watch or to consult, neither of which means investigate.

options.text: The police are looking into the case.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Look into' means to investigate, which is what an investigation of a case involves.

options.text: The police are looking in on the case.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Look in on' means to visit briefly, which is different from investigating.

questions.explanation:
Several look phrasal verbs differ only in their particle, so the particle must be identified precisely rather than guessed.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly uses 'pick up'.
questions.context: A linguistics exercise examines meaning differences within one particle set.

options.text: Could you pick for up the parcel from the post office?
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Pick for up' separates a particle that must stay with the verb.

options.text: Could you pick up of the parcel from the post office?
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Up of' adds a preposition that is not part of the phrasal verb.

options.text: Could you pick the parcel up on the post office?
options.feedback: Wrong. 'On the post office' would place the parcel on the building, which is a different action.

options.text: Could you pick up the parcel from the post office?
options.feedback: Correct. 'Pick up' can mean to collect something or to learn a language, and here it means to collect a parcel.

questions.explanation: Pick up has several senses, including to collect and to acquire a skill, and the surrounding words determine which one applies.
